speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: URANIUM
subtopic: REPORT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH FRENCH GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the House is aware I returned over the week end from a visit to Paris, where I held discussions with Ministers of the French Government regarding uranium. At the conclusion of the discussions the following joint communique was issued on May 22:
The French Secretary of State for Scientific, Atomic and Space Affairs, Mr. Yvon Bourges, and the Canadian Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Honourable Mitchell Sharp, have concluded today a series of talks on matters pertaining to a sale of uranium by Canada to France. In the opinion of the Canadian and French Ministers, these discussions should be viewed in the context of increasing co-operation between the two countries, which has been witnessed at other recent talks at ministerial level.
The purpose of the discussions concerning a proposed sale of uranium was to provide for a first exchange of views at ministerial level on the main questions involved in the provision by Canada of fuel required for France's rapidly expanding program of nuclear reactors for the production of electrical power. The ministers noted with satisfaction that the discussions had been of great value to both sides in the examination of various aspects of the proposed sale.
The two ministers will report to their governments on their conversations.
This concludes the communique. For the information of hon. Members may I add the following points by way of clarification. At these meetings in Paris we did not attempt to negotiate a contract of sale for Canadian uranium. We were concerned only with the general conditions under which a sale could be negotiated and under which uranium could be exported from Canada by producers. As hon. Members are no doubt aware, the export of uranium from Canada requires the approval of the Government.
I made it clear during the discussions that in accordance with the firm policy of the Canadian Government, the proposed sale of uranium could be only for peaceful purposes. As the communique indicates, the French Government for its part is interested in acquiring Canadian uranium for its civil program of nuclear reactors for the production of electrical power.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: URANIUM
subtopic: REPORT ON DISCUSSIONS WITH FRENCH GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
The report given by the Minister has one quality; it frankly faces the situation and does not build up any false hopes. Indeed, as one reads between the lines one can only conclude that there are very great difficulties in the way of securing from the Republic of France an order for uranium of the dimensions in question. I should like at some time for the Minister to let the House know whether during these discussions the Government pf Canada advanced the view that it was prepared to alter the basis upon which Great Britain and the United States today are able to acquire uranium; in other words, to make changes in the arrangements that go back almost to the end of the last war, these changes to be made in order to bring about a possible agreement with the Republic of France.
I hope, Sir, that the changes are not made, and that Canada takes the firm and definite stand on the matter as reported by the Minister a few moments ago, that any sales that will be made will be clearly based upon the agreement that the uranium shall be used for peaceful purposes. This reassurance on the part of the Minister is in accordance with the general stand that Canada has taken through the years.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure hon. Members appreciate the fact that the Minister has given us a preliminary report on his initial discussions with the representatives of the French Government regarding a possible contract for the sale of uranium by Canada. I am sure Members in all parts of the House hope it will be possible to successfully work out an agreement whereby Canada will be able to sell large quantities of uranium, thereby stimulating the uranium industry and bringing employment to those parts of the country that have been adversely affected by the decline in the uranium market in recent years.
There are three points, Mr. Speaker, about which I hope the Government will be able to give us information at an early date. The

Proposed TJranium Sale to France first is one the Minister has already mentioned. We are glad he stated that Canada will take a very firm position that any uranium sold by this country must be for peaceful purposes. Such an agreement must provide for adequate inspection and control, and some form of machinery must be set up to make absolutely sure that uranium sold to France, or to any other country, is used entirely for civil purposes. This is particularly important in this case because France is one country that has refused to sign the partial nuclear test ban agreement, and I think there would be some public reaction if adequate safeguards were not taken to make sure that any Canadian uranium sold to France was going to be confined entirely to civil purposes.
The second point on which I would like to get some information from the Minister at an early date is with respect to the length of the agreement. It is to be hoped it will be a fairly long term agreement. One of the mistakes we made with the U.S. agreements was that they were very short term agreements, and I know that in the Province of Saskatchewan as well as in the Province of Ontario the governments, municipal and provincial, made very large social capital investments on the strength of those agreements. Although we recognized at the time that they were short term agreements we had no choice but to make these very heavy investments in communities which virtually became ghost towns when the agreements ended. If we are going to build up an elaborate structure in Canadian uranium mining it has to be on the basis of long term agreements.
The third point concerns the matter of price. If we are going to get long term agreements, particularly a 25 year agreement in the case of the French contract, I hope the Minister can arrange in such a contract to have a guaranteed price for only a limited period of time, with the price to be renegotiable in the latter part of the life of the agreement.
All the indications are there is going to be an increasing demand for uranium. Experts have forecast that by 1973 there will be a great world demand for uranium, and it is quite conceivable that having a fixed price now for 25 years would find us selling uranium to our customers at a price far below the world price within the 25 year period. If it were possible to get an agreement that would be open ended after a specific period of time, so the price would then be renegotiable, this would be to Canada's advantage.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this party note with interest the report made by the Minister in regard to his negotiations in Paris relating to the sale of Canadian uranium. With the prospects of a vast increase in the world market for uranium as nuclear power becomes more commonplace it is obvious that what we are dealing with is something that is much greater than just Canadian-French relationships at this time. With France as a member of NATO, with the prospects of uranium becoming a very strategic item particularly among NATO countries, certainly the groundwork that is being laid now in these negotiations is something broader than what is being discussed between our two countries.
I noted with interest reports circulating through news media that one of the reasons the Minister was not able to come to any definite conclusion about this sale agreement is that he expects to carry out negotiations with the United States government as well in this regard. It would have been good if the Minister had referred to this. It emphasizes again that we are dealing with a very broad aspect of nuclear power development through the basic material of uranium.
One thing is important in connection with this subject. It is whether there is a satisfactory agreement with France as far as the use of uranium for peaceful purposes is concerned, bearing in mind that whatever uranium France may obtain from Canada now if stockpiled will release other material, not liable to restriction, for military use. I know the Minister is taking this into consideration.
I do not think it is satisfactory to pretend that the whole question is being settled by this trade arrangement which is now being negotiated. Having regard to the tremendous supply of uranium which is available in Canada, we must certainly lead the way in developing some satisfactory proposal for the sale of uranium not only to France but to other countries, a proposal covering not only use but price.
We shall await with interest reports of further negotiations.

Mr. Speaker, the communique issued by the two countries following their discussions and read by the Minister of Trade and Commerce was
May 25. 1965	COMMONS
surely one of the most laconic ones we have ever heard. No conclusion emerged from it and it could even be perceived that the negotiations had not been as successful as the two parties involved expected. This is shown by the fact that the communique contains several statements to the effect that Canada and France are friendly countries, but nothing to suggest that an agreement has been reached. Mention is made that the meeting was not held in order to negotiate a contract, but simply to discuss the conditions of such a contract. In spite of all this, it is impossible to infer that the conditions laid down by each party have been accepted by both of them. Consequently, the communique is far from satisfactory. What is the main reason for the failure of those negotiations?
Well, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Trade and Commerce will admit that, on the one hand, Canada wants to exercise some control and supervision-that is part of the conditions of sale of uranium to France-but, on the other hand, as stated in recent press releases, France wants no part of such control and supervision. However, in the joint communique, France stated that it needed uranium for its nuclear reactors in order to produce electric power. Those are the statements contained in the joint communique; the statement is official enough to be sufficient in itself, I think, especially when it comes from a friendly country such as France, unless France, in the case of this agreement, is not considered as one of the friendly countries mentioned at the beginning of the communique.
Mr. Speaker, I still maintain the position we have already taken in this matter. When negotiations were carried on with Great Britain and the United States, even if they were carried on during the few years after the war, we knew perfectly well to what purpose the uranium would be used, that is for military purposes, but no conditions were imposed on that sale as they are imposed today with respect to another country, a friendly country, France.
I think negotiations should be put on another basis. We should have confidence in the statement made in the joint communique by the Canadian Minister of Trade and Commerce and Mr. Yvon Bourges, on behalf of France, to the effect that this uranium will be used for their nuclear reactors in order to produce electric power. In addition, I think Canada feels the need for such a sale, such a contract, especially to improve its balance

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have another short announcement to make. I have been informed by the Canadian Wheat Board that the Board has concluded negotiations in Hong Kong for the sale to mainland China of 1| million long tons of Canadian wheat, approximately 58,700,000 bushels including shipping tolerance. Further details will be announced by the Canadian Wheat Board within the next few days.

maintopic: WHEAT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SALE TO MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this occasion to say a few words about the China wheat market because of its importance at this time. In the first place I think we can gather from the announcement made today that this is no longer a temporary type of market. I think we have to assume now that this is not a windfall type of arrangement but will be here permanently.
Therefore, in view of its importance I am going to ask the Minister and the Government to take effective action with regard to the desire of mainland China to set up in this country, as they have in other countries, an unofficial trade office where their representatives can meet with Canadian businessmen, so we can show some honest effort on our part to get their goods into this country, which 
are not coming in in any amount at all at the present time.

maintopic: WHEAT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SALE TO MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: WHEAT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SALE TO MAINLAND CHINA
speechtext:
The second point I want to make is that at the Canton trade fair which ended just last week, of some 5,000 businessmen there from all over the world only a handful were Canadian. I think the Department of Trade and Commerce has to make just as much effort to enter into this market as we make with regard to other markets, and I think we should have several hundred businessmen organized to go to the coming trade fairs in April, May and September to make sure that Canadians know what the Chinese are producing.
I am not going to discuss price at this time because that comes under the purview of the wheat board. It is their business and the business of the farmers; therefore we should not talk about it here.
My final point is this. Trade with China is not going to be a one way street. We are selling them approximately $150 million worth of wheat a year and we are buying back a handful of millions-$4 million or $5 million-of dollars worth of materials. Canadian policy should be to help the Chinese in every way to establish legitimate trade relations with us, and at the same time Canadian Government policy should be to persuade the Americans themselves to change their regulations and their act to allow American businessmen to trade with China as well. If this kind of approach were taken by the Minister I am sure he would find that some ears in the United States would be willing to listen, and we could hope that the American rules and regulations, and their act as a matter of fact, aimed against the American citizens who trade with China, would be amended or removed so that American business could make contact with this great country. When we remember that 70 per cent to 80 per cent of our business is entangled with American business, the importance of this matter to Canada is obvious.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I would take this opportunity to ask the Government to realize that this China trade is no longer a windfall, as the Prime Minister said when in opposition. It is a permanent arrangement and we must protect that permanent arrangement, not only for wheat but for all the other products the Chinese want. The slogan to keep in mind is "A single market of 700 million people under single management".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise for the purpose of making a motion on a matter of 
urgent public importance which is, as I see it, of such emergency that it requires immediate debate.
As you know, for quite some time Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition has been asking for a day to be set aside for the discussion of matters of international importance concerned with the peace of the world. Indeed, in the light of events in the last two days and the kaleidoscopic changes that are taking place internationally, a discussion of international affairs can no longer be delayed.
In respect of the urgency involved I have only to mention the fact that in the past 48 hours the press has reported that plans are now under way to bring the equivalent of a United States army combat division into South Viet Nam. This is according to informed U.S. mission sources.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, we have received a report today from Cyrus Eaton who at all times in recent years has been loud in his protestations of good relationships between the western world and the U.S.S.R. He has returned from a visit to the U.S.S.R. and has stated, among other things, that during his meeting in the Kremlin with Premier Alexis Kosygin last Thursday he was terrified by this man's attitude; that he had never met a man so grim, so wrought up or so serious. Kosygin told him "You have left us no alternative but to fight".
I use that reference because throughout the last several years Mr. Eaton has had that closeness of relationship with Mr. Khrushchev which impelled him to say that so long as Khrushchev was in charge of the U.S.S.R. there would be no danger of war.
As I have mentioned, Sir, we have tried to obtain information, but it is quite impossible to do so. No matter how comprehensive the answers given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs we are entirely in the dark in this matter, which far transcends any question normally of a domestic nature. We are left with a labyrinth of words while the world situation is deteriorating and gradually becoming worse. I need not point out what happened in Viet Nam within the last two days. As reported by authoritative British sources, the Viet Cong has taken over control of rural areas. This being a matter which requires consideration by Parliament, the Canadian people must not be kept in the dark.
Furthermore, what took place in the Dominican Republic over the week end has induced Mr. U Thant to state that the United Nations was being ignored; and the Prime
May 25, 1965



Minister, in one of his extramural statements, indicated that he was in agreement with that view. Indeed, too often the information we get on external affairs today is that given outside the House in the course of speeches. At the same time the Shah of Iran spoke of the weakness of the United Nations.
I could mention other matters of immediate importance. There is the situation regarding NATO, where the indications are that General de Gaulle has a plan of withdrawal. On the other hand we had the Prime Minister's statement in Sudbury which to say the least was critical of the course being taken by the President of the French Republic. In the past 48 hours, as Canada's leaders have paraded before the international footlights, we have had to get our information through radio and television broadcasts. The Secretary of State for External Affairs was quoted as having indicated that there were discussions on the transfer of the United Nations headquarters or some of its agencies to Montreal, and within 24 hours the hon. gentleman said the report was incorrect. Finally, in the past 48 hours there has been a report that Canada may be denied defence information by NORAD.
These statements all indicate that the time has come for a debate so we may learn what the situation is and not have to depend on statements regarding these matters made by various incognitos in other parts of the world.
I therefore ask leave, under Standing Order 26, to move the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the alarm and uncertainty which today prevail in the country with respect to strained world relations in general and in particular as to (a) the dangerous developments in Viet Nam and the Dominican Republic; (b) the uncertainty as to the future of NATO, with particular reference to the future participation of France; (c) the use and control of tactical nuclear weapons by NATO forces; (d) the uncertainty as to the future role of Canada in continental defence within NORAD; and
(e)	the new uncertainties facing the position of the United Nations, which alarm and uncertainty stem from the Government's continuing refusal to give clear information on these matters, its confused and equivocal handling of these situations and the collapse of Canada's traditionally effective role in international politics.
I say, Sir, that the urgency is apparent to anyone who reads the headlines, and I ask
External Affairs
therefore that this matter receive the attention of the House.

Mr. Speaker, the right hon. gentleman has asked leave to move the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance. There is no question about the importance of this matter. Because it deals with the question of peace and war it is perhaps more important than any other subject that can be brought before us.
There is some doubt in my own mind as to the definiteness of the matter having in mind points (a) (b) (c) (d) and (e), all of which deal in a very general way with foreign policy, and there remains the question of urgency.
The right hon. gentleman has stated that there is evidence of the worsening of the international situation in an alarming way, and this therefore means that the matter is so urgent it should be discussed today and that we should interrupt our ordinary business for that purpose. We have no evidence before us, Mr. Speaker, of the worsening of the situation in that alarming and critical way to which reference has been made.
There are, of course, ways in which this matter could be discussed. If we could deal with the parliamentary reform resolutions now before us we could set up the Committee on External Affairs immediately and there could be a full discussion in that committee. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, if the resolution concerning that matter is not passed we can always, by unanimous consent, set up the Committee on External Affairs at once. We can also arrange with the house leaders to have a supply debate next Monday when this question can be brought forward if the Opposition so desires.
But, Mr. Speaker, I am not arguing, of course, against the importance of this matter or against the desirability of a debate at this time provided Your Honour feels it is a matter of urgent public importance. If you make that decision, Mr. Speaker, we will be very glad indeed to take part in a debate today.

The second point has to do with the question of urgency. In that regard I would remind the Prime Minister that on the last supply motion the hon. We have had no statements whatsoever with regard to where the Canadian Government stands on the matter of Viet Nam. We are a member of the truce commission which has been completely overlooked and neglected. The situation in the last week or 10 days in the Dominican Republic has caused a good deal of concern in Canada in view of the fact that this country, located as it is in the western hemisphere, is affected by anything that happens in the Caribbean. In addition, as clause (e) of the motion points out, throughout this entire series of unfortunate incidents the United Nations has been bypassed completely by unilateral action on the part of the United States.
It seems to me that the Canadian Government should give a clear expression of its views with respect to these various troubled spots in the world. I do not think we can afford to delay this matter. The Government has not provided any opportunity for discussion. It has not called any of the estimates and has not done any of the things that would provide an opportunity for debate. I believe that on April 2 there was a brief debate on foreign policy on a supply motion, but apart from that there has been no debate. I think there can be no better time than the present, when the world situation calls for some leadership on the part of the Canadian Government, to have a full scale debate and to give the House an opportunity to express its opinion

with respect to the various items that have been listed in the motion moved by the Leader of the Opposition.

maintopic: WHEAT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SALE TO MAINLAND CHINA
subsubtopic: OPPORTUNITY FOR DEBATE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
There is no question in the minds of the members of this party but that it would be desirable to have a discussion in this House on foreign affairs, particularly with regard to the situation that has developed in Viet Nam and in the Dominican Republic as well as other places in the world. We think we can agree that there has not been sufficient information given to this House with regard to these trouble spots in the world. The question immediately arises, Mr. Speaker, has the Secretary of State for External Affairs more information that he is at liberty to give to this House?
It is not fair to say that no information has been given, because there have been a number of occasions when the Minister has attempted to give what I should like to call "sop" information to the House respecting these two matters. It is rather difficult, because while we agree that more information ought to be given, while we agree that there is a very serious situation in the world that we would like to see helped, the fact is that we have to abide by the rules of this House. It is your duty and obligation, Mr. Speaker, to enforce these rules.
Citation 100 reads in part as follows:
The definite matter of urgent public importance for the discussion of which a Member may ask leave to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 must involve the administrative responsibility of the Government.
I cannot see anything in the motion moved by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition that directly involves the administrative responsibility of this Government. I can understand your position therefore, Mr. Speaker, and the quandary in which you will be if you are going to apply the rules that have been given to you by this House and at the same time take into account the importance of this matter.
Then, of course, the motion refers also to the alarm and uncertainty which today prevails in the country with respect to strained world conditions in general. The motion then lists five items. Well, Mr. Speaker, this may be definite but it is certainly not a specific thing. Paragraph (2) of citation 100 reads in part as follows:
The "definite matter of urgent public importance", for the discussion of which the adjournment of the House may be moved under Standing Order 26, must be so pressing that public interest will suffer if it is not given immediate attention.
May 25, 1965

I contend, Mr. Speaker, that we can argue, debate and discuss these generalities in the motion moved by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition all day, but that would not necessarily assist the public interest in this matter.
Then the "urgency" within this rule does not apply to the matter itself but means urgency of debate. Of course, Mr. Speaker, you are familiar with this citation. It means that the public interest demands that a discussion take place immediately, and that something useful in the public interest can come out of this debate. This is what is meant when reference is made to urgency.
Another point you may look at, Mr. Speaker, is contained in paragraph (5) of citation 100. This does not apply particularly to matters in the international field, but I think we can draw a parallel between that and the national field. I quote:
The adjournment of the House cannot be moved with reference to critical conditions generally prevailing in certain parts of the country.
I think this paragraph can be applied so that the adjournment of the House cannot be moved under this rule for critical conditions prevailing generally in certain parts of the world. Notwithstanding the tremendous importance to all Canadians of these trouble spots in Viet Nam and the Dominican Republic, it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that you have no choice if you are to apply the rules that were given to you by this House, and you will have to rule this matter out of order.
I hope we can get on with passing the two resolutions on procedure that are before the House, so we can get the standing committees of this House realigned as quickly as possible. Then I believe, although I have not checked, that the Department of External Affairs has already been entered and could be referred to the Standing Committee. It seems to me that it is in this Standing Committee that the Minister of External Affairs could be called and cross-examined so we could get all the information he is free to give to Members of this House respecting these critical situations in the world.
I hope, therefore, that we can follow this line of action because, important as this matter raised in the motion of the Leader of the Opposition is, it seems to me that it would be a clear violation of the rules under Standing Order 26 to accept the motion. We in this party have always taken the position that we do have to support the Speaker
External Affairs
and support the rules that are given to the Speaker. This is our position, as we see it, in this instance.

maintopic: WHEAT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SALE TO MAINLAND CHINA
subsubtopic: OPPORTUNITY FOR DEBATE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on reading the motion moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), I am inclined to agree with the Prime Minister when he states that the motion does not concern the discussion of a definite matter. In fact, when reading the motion one finds that the terms contradict one another.
The Leader of the Opposition is asking to discuss:
-a definite matter-
And that definite matter is:
-the alarm and uncertainty-
Mr. Speaker, I wonder how uncertainty can be definite. Only certainty can become definite. Therefore, the Leader of the Opposition would have to tell us first what is uncertain and what is definite, and then we would be able to decide if this motion is in order.
He wants to discuss a definite matter, and that is exactly what he wishes to discuss. Even if alarm and uncertainty do exist, uncertainty still remains something which one cannot determine or define. All along he referred to uncertainty as to the United Nations, as to the future role of Canada. The future is another thing which cannot be considered as a definite matter, since nobody has the divinatory power to determine the future. Therefore, the future cannot be considered as a definite matter.
There is also reference to uncertainty as to NATO's future. The motion before us is obviously not on a definite matter. Of course, as was pointed out by the right hon. Prime Minister a moment ago, we would be interested in a general debate on external affairs, but I do not believe we should delay the business of the house to consider this motion of the Leader of the Opposition.
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition bases his motion on standing order 26 (2), but I wish to draw his attention to standing order 26 (6) (b), which reads as follows:
Not more than one matter can be discussed on the same motion;
Now, we are called upon to discuss the situation in Viet Nam and in the Dominican Republic. These two countries are so far from each other that they constitute two different matters.

May 25. 1965
External Affairs
We are also asked to deal with NATO, NORAD and the United Nations. These are three different organizations and should not be dealt as one matter.
We are also asked to deal with the future, the past and the present state of uncertainty. There again, the motion aims at discussing more than one matter.
Mr. Speaker, we, in our group, are ready to adjourn the house to discuss urgent matters but only with regard to domestic matters. In fact, the debate now proposed will not settle the problems in Viet Nam, in the Dominican Republic, in NATO, in NORAD or in the United Nations. It is going to take more than one day to settle all that. Furthermore, to discuss all these problems today will do nothing to settle those existing at present in all those parts of the world.
Mr. Speaker, what surprises me most are the following words I find in the motion moved by the Leader of the Opposition:
-which alarm and uncertainty stem from the government's continuing refusal to give clear information on these matters-
Mr. Speaker, as if whether or not the government gives us information is going to settle the war in Viet Nam and the rebellion in the Dominican Republic. In my opinion, whatever information we may get this is not what is going to settle those problems.
We feel that there are more important things to settle than matters concerning Viet Nam and the Dominican Republic. Moreover, if those matters are discussed, what we will have will be mere talk, not a debate. As far as we are concerned we want to discuss matters concerning Canada.
I know that the Leader of the Opposition is facing some difficulties within his party and that he would like to discuss matters concerning certain foreign countries, but we prefer to solve the problems before us in Canada, and we suggest that this is what we should do.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I merely want to say that in my opinion, the remarks of the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) show a parochial spirit and indicate that he has misunderstood the meaning of the motion introduced by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), Therefore, I will restrict myself to that description of the remarks of the hon. member.

With respect to the hon. Member for Medicine Hat, I find it passing strange that

he would advance as his concluding argument that all the rules he cited and the arguments put forward in Beauchesne- which is nothing more than a commentary- must strengthen Your Honour's hand in matters of this kind. I do not think the hon. Member, on reflection, would like that argument to remain as he put it, because I do not think there is anything required within the rules to strengthen Your Honour's hand one way or the other in deciding whether proceedings shall be adjourned under Standing Order 26.
Neither do I think one needs to spend any great length of time on the preliminary arguments put forward by the Prime Minister, and I think he also on reflection would wish to back away from them; because I believe he too would see there is a precise point in regard to this motion, with respect to the alarm and uncertainty in the country about the situation. His colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs will certainly agree they are important; and if there is alarm and uncertainty as a result of events, then that must be dealt with by the Government.
With respect to the question of urgency of debate-and I think this is the main problem facing Your Honour-it has been argued that this is a continuing situation which the House had the opportunity to discuss in the past. I would put it to Your Honour that this has not been the case. We have dealt with this at some distance away in point of time in the debate on the Speech from the Throne. Then there was the budget debate, and there have been other specific matters and debates during which the House has not had the opportunity to discuss this particular item.
It is not open to the Government to call the first item in external affairs estimates without going into a supply motion. The Prime Minister said we could by unanimous consent go into a supply motion-

subsubtopic: OPPORTUNITY FOR DEBATE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Not today.

subsubtopic: OPPORTUNITY FOR DEBATE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Unanimous consent would be required today. By unanimous consent we could deal with the matter, and I put it to the right hon. gentleman that the House giving unanimous consent would be tantamount to the same thing the motion proposes.
With respect to the Prime Minister saying "Well, we could call a supply motion in the future," for example say next Monday, I point out that the Leader of the Opposition and the House are not aware of the Government's attitude until this statement is made, and it is a statement made under duress of
May 25. 1965

the motion and has not been announced beforehand. Therefore the Opposition is quite in order in putting forward this motion to try to elicit a stand from the Government in this regard.
Further with respect to opportunities for debate, I must say I find it passing strange not only with the hon. Member for Medicine Hat but with the Prime Minister and his followers that if we were to go on to adopt the package deal of resolutions in motions No. 14 and 15 on the order paper, then we could get to this particular question. Surely to goodness in his responsible position the Prime Minister will not for one moment suggest that we should gloss over the very important and complicated matter of amendments to procedure in the House in order to get at this particular question. He might as well say "Well, pass the order paper, the whole of the order paper, then we will get to the question."

maintopic: WHEAT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SALE TO MAINLAND CHINA
subsubtopic: OPPORTUNITY FOR DEBATE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: WHEAT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SALE TO MAINLAND CHINA

speechtext:
The argument is just as valid. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I put it to you that this motion to adjourn the House meets with the requirement of precision, meets the requirement of national importance, and certainly meets what I would say is the paramount requirement of urgency of debate.
If we look at the items that are indicated in the motion we see we have the situation with regard to France's participation in NATO. This is a rather recent matter so far as the public is concerned, and there are the implications of the ministerial statement issued after the Ministers' conference. Then there is the question which came to the fore this past week end, of Secretary McNamara's statement with respect to a change of policy regarding tactical nuclear weapons available to forces in Europe. Then there is the matter of the United Nations, and the Minister's statement the other day as to the site of the United Nations.
All these matters give rise to uncertainty, and we ask the Minister to stand on his feet, assume his responsibilities and make a statement to the House.

maintopic: WHEAT-ANNOUNCEMENT OF SALE TO MAINLAND CHINA
subsubtopic: OPPORTUNITY FOR DEBATE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Order, please. I wish to thank hon. Members who have taken part in this short discussion. It is of material benefit in assisting the Chair to reach what I hope is a right decision.
I accept the proposition that this is an urgent and important public matter to which the Leader of the Opposition draws attention. It is a definite
External Affairs
matter of public importance. However, that is not the criterion in determining whether Standing Order 26 should be applied. The criterion is whether there is an opportunity to debate this matter in an effective way.
Those words are the words of a previous Speaker who had a similar situation in which to render judgment, on June 27, 1961, and the statement can be found in greater detail at page 7105 of Hansard for that date. It was the decision of Mr. Speaker Michener.
There is no doubt about the importance of the various subjects detailed in the motion, but under Standing Order 26 it seems to me the question is, is there an opportunity to debate these matters in an effective way?
If hon. Members would refer to Beau-chesne, citation 100, subparagraphs (1) (2) (3) and (8)-I do not think there is any need to detail them here; they are reasonably clear-they will find they serve as a guide. Although the matters referred to are extremely important and of great national interest, my decision has to be based on whether or not they are of such recent origin, of such recent urgency, that all the business of the House must be set aside in order that they may be discussed.
There is no doubt, it seems to me, that these are extremely important questions, but it has been indicated that there could be a supply motion on Monday, and various other suggestions have been made. Also, if we were to set aside all the business on the agenda this afternoon I doubt very much whether we would affect the course of events dealt with in the motion. I cannot, therefore, conclude that this is an emergency requiring all the business of the House to be set aside, and accede to the request made by the Leader of the Opposition.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
wish to thank the hon. Member for bringing this question forward and also to mention that this question was asked by the hon. Member for Grey-Bruce on the 20th and 21st of May. The answer to this question is longer than would normally be given in answer to a question on orders of the day. However, in view of the importance of the question to the livestock industry I wonder whether I may have the indulgence of the House to read the complete statement.
On May 20 and 21 the hon. Member for Grey-Bruce raised certain questions in connection with importations of European cattle into Canada. The Minister would like to reply to these questions in some detail, since this program is of considerable importance to the livestock industry in Canada. The matter is of interest at the present time because of suggestions in some quarters in the United States that if these European importations take place shipments of Canadian livestock and meats into the United States should be banned.
Let me say first that we are satisfied that there is no risk of introducing disease into this country as a result of this program and that we have had no indication, in consultations with United States Government officials about this program, that it could lead to any restriction of Canadian livestock exports to the United States. I am confident that any suggestions that our livestock and meats should be banned from the United States are based on a misunderstanding of our proposed program.
Canada, along with most countries, controls imports of livestock and meat to the extent

DEBATES	May 25, 1965
necessary to prevent the introduction of serious foreign diseases. In keeping with this policy there has been a complete ban on the importation of animals and uncooked meats from most countries in Europe and elsewhere. The United States has had similar restrictions.
One of the main diseases both our countries have been concerned about is foot and mouth disease, and I am sure every thinking person agrees that health restrictions of this nature are necessary. But I think there is also agreement that these restrictions should not be applied to the point of restricting imports of blood lines which may be useful to our livestock industry, if such imports can be made with complete safety.
England, for example, has periodic outbreaks of foot and mouth disease. It is controlled there as we would control it here, by slaughtering infected herds. But Canada for years has been permitting the import of English cattle as long as they go through the quarantine station in Scotland, which has historically been free of the disease. English cattle are not permitted to be imported directly into the United States because of certain provisions in United States animal health laws. But for years many American breeders have imported British cattle by bringing them in through Canada.
Both Canada and the United States have recently taken steps which recognize that under reliable health controls and testing procedures importations can be made which carry no danger of bringing in disease. The United States has approached this problem by authorizing the importation of semen from all countries whether they are completely free of foot and mouth disease or not. Semen, of course, can carry the foot and mouth virus just as readily as live animals. But health controls and testing procedures have been developed which can give complete protection against the introduction of infection in this kind of program.
The United States has dealt with semen rather than animals because its laws specifically prohibit animal imports from countries which are not entirely free of foot and mouth disease. Canadian laws are more flexible in this respect and permit us to import animals as long as this is done with adequate health precautions. We will, however, import only from countries where foot and mouth disease is under control.
The only country from which such imports are proposed at present is France. Since 1961 France has had a policy of slaughtering
May 25, 1965	COMMONS
herds if foot and mouth disease occurs. It also vaccinates all calves against the disease. In the last two years French breeding cattle have been exported to some 30 countries without any difficulties on health grounds. These include Ireland, which like Canada is historically free of foot and mouth disease and which has an important meat and cattle trade into the United States.
I should like now to give some details of the procedures that will be followed because I believe they will make clear that we have taken every precaution in this program. First, any cattle which come to Canada must come from areas in which there has been no foot and mouth disease, even though the French do slaughter in such outbreaks. We will take only calves and they must not be vaccinated against foot and mouth disease. The animals will be disease tested while they are still on the French owner's premises, including a test for foot and mouth disease. They will then move into the French quarantine station at Brest for 30 days where they will be further tested. Following that they will come to the security quarantine station in Canada at Grosse-ile. Our regulations require quarantine here for a period of 90 days but in most cases it will be up to five months. They will again be tested at the Canadian station.
All the blood samples are to be sent to the foot and mouth disease research institute at Pirbright, England, to be tested for foot and mouth disease. This is one of the outstanding research stations for that disease in the world, and the whole program has been developed with the co-operation of the authorities there. We are completely satisfied that this program involves no risk of introducing foot and mouth disease into Canada and that American livestock interests need have no concern on this score.
The United States authorities have been kept fully informed of our program. There has been agreement on the soundness of the procedures which we will follow and there has been no indication in the consultations with American officials that, under those procedures, there would be any health grounds for restrictions on the movement of Canadian cattle or meat to the United States.
The trade between the two countries in livestock and meats is by no means a one way street. In recent years, for example, we have been importing more pork from the United States than we have been exporting to that country. In 1964 our imports were 54 million pounds and our exports 42 million 22620-104
DEBATES	1619
Inquiries of the Ministry pounds. Our exports of beef and veal and slaughter and feeder cattle in 1964 were, in terms of carcass weight, 88 million pounds, while our imports for the first 11 months were 30 million pounds.
We have invited the American authorities to have their own veterinary observer present with ours during all phases of our program. We recognize that in livestock and meats we are on a North American economy and obviously we must not take any steps which would expose the continent to disease. I am also sure that the Americans do not want to encourage any action that might be restrictive to Canada on anything but sound animal health grounds.
We are each very dependant on the other in agricultural trade. In total, imports of United States agricultural products into Canada are over twice as great as the value of Canadian agricultural exports to the United States. The last available complete figures for 1963 show agricultural imports from the United States to Canada at a total value of $513 million while Canadian exports to the United States were only $223 million.

The House resumed from Friday, May 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Knowles, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Olson:
That this House recognize the need for improving its procedures to provide full opportunity for the critical examination of proposed legislation and to ensure the effective dispatch of public business;
That this House agrees upon the need for allocating the time for the business of the House;
and	.
That, in order to secure improved examination of the details of legislation and of public spending, while maintaining the full authority of the House, this House agrees upon the value of making increased use of Standing Committees;
That this House accordingly orders:
1. That detailed examination of estimates, saving always the right of the Committee of Supply, be undertaken by Standing Committees and that not more than 36 days of the time of the House be allocated to the business of supply in each session. For the purpose of this order, the business of supply shall consist of proceedings on motions "That Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair"; supplementary or additional estimates for the financial year; interim supply; and main estimates whether for the coming or the current financial year. That a Special Committee of the House, consisting of twenty-two members, to be designated later by the House, be instructed to prepare and to submit to the House forthwith the changes in Standing Orders consequential upon this order, including any means of giving to the opposition an opportunity to select the departmental estimates to be discussed.
May 25, 1965	COMMONS
2. That the Standing Orders be amended by adding thereto a new Standing Order 15-A, to read as follow:
Standing Order 15-A
15-A. (1) There shall be a Business Committee to which the leader of each party in the House from time to time by written notice to the Speaker may appoint one member.
(2)	During routine proceedings a Minister of the Crown may request that the question of allocation of time for consideration of any item of business or stage thereof be referred to the Business Committee for consideration and report, and upon such request being made such question shall stand referred to the committee.
(3)	The Business Committee shall report back to the House on or before the third sitting day following such request.
(4)	If the Chairman of the Business Committee reports that the committee has unanimously recommended an allocation of time for the item of business or stage thereof, a Minister of the Crown may without notice propose a motion, to be decided without debate or amendment, for concurrence in the report, and if agreed to, the motion shall have the same effect as if it were an order of the House.
(5)	If the Chairman of the Business Committee reports that the committee has been unable to reach a unanimous agreement or if the committee fails to report within the time specified by Section (3) of this Standing Order, a Minister of the Crown
may give notice that at the next sitting of the House he will move that an order be made allocating the time for the item of business or stage thereof.
(6)	A motion of which a Minister has given notice under Section (5) of this Standing Order shall be made during routine proceedings. Unless the debate on the motion has been previously concluded, Mr. Speaker shall at fifteen minutes before the expiry of the time provided for Government business in such sitting interrupt the proceedings and forthwith put every question necessary to dispose of the main motion. A motion requesting allocation of time, if agreed to, shall have the same effect as if it were an order of the House.-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I followed on Friday the quiet, calm, reasoned and sometimes low-keyed debate on this important matter which, according to some members of the press, was supposed to topple kingdoms and unleash the party legions, I thought how different actuality frequently is from such predictions. I agree so much with what the hon. Member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) said on Friday that these continual predictions of elections are not only irritating but they are somewhat boring, at least they are to me because I have never believed any of them. It is my own view that the snows of at least one winter will come and go before this Government will go to the country. When I hear all of the threats I am reminded of the expression, the mouse that roared, because I think
DEBATES	1621
House of Commons Procedures the Government does exercise good judgment in not rushing to the people for a rendering of a judgment on their performance.
Now, I have no inside information on this. I did not get a chance to write to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). I was not asked, but if he does ask me I shall send him my views on what should be done. I hope, however, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) suggested, on this very important matter there will be a free vote. One hears not only in this Parliament but in every parliament where matters of procedure are dis-cusssed, the reiteration that everybody wants to improve the procedure. This is a point on which there is agreement. Everybody wants a more effective Parliament. It would strike me as doubtful if there would be basic grounds for a party point of view on matters of procedure, some of them as detailed, precise and possibly as intricate as those involved in the subject matter before us. One can see a party taking the point of view on questions of principle, but surely not on a matter of procedure.
I should say, however, that in rendering this view I am not saying that it indicates at all an attitude on my part-I speak only for myself-of reluctance if someone is desirous of taking a measure, whether it be a measure of this kind or any other, to the ultimate question of confidence and of the results that flow from a negative vote thereon. On any matters of importance, which I believe are inimical to the nature and role of an opposition, any opposition in parliament and thus to parliament itself, I would not hesitate to oppose to the ultimate.
It is true that, as other speakers have mentioned, we are becoming very concerned about our image. I hope we are doing a little more than looking in the mirror. To use an old fashioned expression, I hope we are looking into our hearts as well. There are times- and the hon. Member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) mentioned this the other day-when parliamentarians discuss their institution that they sound so lofty it would seem rules would not be necessary at all. Then there are times when we behave in such a way as to lead one to believe that the most rigid rules are probably not quite stringent enough. But that is the kind of institution parliament is. We go from heights to depths, and I suppose no assemblage of mortals could be otherwise.
I believe there are some reasons why, at this time in our national political development, certain things have happened. I am cer-
1622	COMMONS
House of Commons Procedures tainly not a veteran of the House of Commons, although after eight years I feel sometimes, if not experienced at least old; but I have the impression that in the short period I have been here inept organization of procedure- and for this the Government must take prime responsibility-has exacerbated our difficulties.
We have had frequent changes of House Leaders. We have had a constant uncertainty as to any long-range plans detailing what the House will be taking up for consideration. We have had a most unfortunate deterioration in the handling of order paper questions. One does not like to reflect on anyone but, as we experienced today, the oral question period does sometimes become too long.
There are many Members who on most occasions would prefer to put their questions on the order paper: By doing this one can lay them a little more precisely and hope to get more precise answers; but the answers are not coming to us.
Last May I asked a question about what the Government planned to do on January 15 to celebrate Sir John A. Macdonald's birthday. It was not a tremendously vital question that would require continuous cabinet meetings to resolve, but I did not get a reply to it until long after his birthday had come and gone. From May to February that fairly simple and straightforward question sat there, without reply. There are many others like it, and this discourages the use of a very important vehicle, namely the order paper, through which precise information should be obtainable.
I think too-and this may sound strange- that as well as a disordered order paper we have one that in recent years has become too heavy. Too many things are being pushed before parliament. We have had so many elections, so many promises, so much promised legislation held before the people. Then this legislation is laid before parliament, and we are expected to enact it in 60 days, or some other very short period of time.
Quite often in this day and age, when welfare is so important, measures that come before us are not completely within the jurisdiction of our Parliament. We had great difficulty over the Canada Pension Plan on that very account, and it was not the only piece of legislation to encounter that problem. Federal parties make promises to do things which do not lie in federal jurisdiction, and it is therefore not surprising that the procedures of this Parliament become involved.
[Mr. Macquarrie.l
DEBATES	May 25, 1965
I believe it is a mistake to regard the passing of legislation as the only function of the House of Commons or of parliament. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), like the old professor he is, quoted Sir Walter Bage-hot. We all did in our classrooms, as our students know. But Bagehot, as I recall, listed five functions of parliament, and he listed four before he even came to legislation. The first one was that of an electoral chamber. It is a body which must sustain a government. Once in a while we have this role activated. We have had in recent times, but not often.
Then Bagehot says it has an expressive function. It must express the minds of the people on all questions. It must be a representative organ. We were a representative parliament before we had responsible government, and by that I mean in the strict sense of the government being responsible to parliament for its continuing confidence. This is a very difficult role, a very important one, and it is with this representative role that we must be concerned when anything happens to diminish the role of the spokesmen for all parts of the country-the backbenchers.
He also said that the House has a teaching function:
A great and open council of considerable men cannot be placed in the middle of a society without altering that society.
At least our public today are concerned about what we are doing here. There are probably more Canadians than ever before who know we are here. This is at least a beginning of an improvement in this field. People are becoming more sensitive, more aware of their national representative institution.
I would not presume to say what Bagehot also stated about Parliament:
It ought to teach the nation what it does not know.
That would be too presumptuous for one who sought public office.
Bagehot said the fourth function of the House was an informing function. In early days the King had to be informed. Now the people are sovereign and they have to be informed, and hence have laid before the nation those things of moment to it.
Finally he mentioned the legislative function, but it seems to me in recent sessions we have been so crowded with legislation that we have begun to suffer in the other roles, the expressive role, the role of careful scrutiny of estimates, and this Government has been
May 25, 1965

very guilty, very remiss in its handling of estimates.
The voting of supply is a preduty to that of passing legislation. It is the fundamental and historic function of a free Parliament.
There are indications that the present suggested procedural change is not nearly as broad as it might be, in that there are many other areas in which I think change would be helpful to a more efficient parliament, and in one or two cases the suggested change goes a little too deeply. In the brief time at my disposal I would like to mention some of these matters.
I believe one of our difficulties is that we have not yet come up with an arrangement whereby we can terminate our sessions. We never know when we are going to end them. In the past session or two we have had a great exercise in the type of suggestion, "Now, if these things are passed we might have an adjournment." Then a little later on the list gets longer and we are told, "If these things are passed we might have an adjournment." Barring a great national emergency I think there is no reason why the House of Commons should meet in July and August. There is no argument that cannot be resumed in September or October. No matter what is done we will hardly ever run out of material for argumentation.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
We must reach a point at which we decide beforehand when we intend to terminate. I would say we should always be out of here in time to celebrate St. Jean Baptiste Day and come back after Labour Day. This might be a good way of doing it and perhaps other adjournments could be fixed, too, at other times of the year, short ones. We must always recognize that we are at a stage in our political life which is complex and involved, that politics are becoming a full time business and that we might as well be rational and businesslike in setting out times for adjournments. The committee report hit the idea, but I believe the suggestion the committee made was not a good one inasmuch as it would have meant too frequent gyrations back and forth between the constituencies and the seat of Government in Ottawa.
Parliaments at the present time are suffering from too constant attendance by Members in Ottawa. Only part of our job can be done here. The most important part is that which must be done in the constituency.
In this connection the question of absenteeism has drawn the attention of the press and there are some reporters who attach such

House of Commons Procedures great importance to the number of Members who are present when votes are taken that they consider this calculation an exhaustive discussion of political matters. I submit that this approach is not satisfactory. I am in the happy position of being able to mention this subject without embarrassment or special pleading, because I think I would get a gold star for attendance this session if prizes were awarded; I do not think I have missed a vote or a day.

speechtext:
I mention this matter to indicate that the problem of absenteeism is resulting in part from the continuing long sessions. How can a Member be here 12 or 13 months of the year, if I may use that expression, without finding time to deal with constituency matters. He must at least show up for his annual meeting, if for nothing else, and these meetings are not always held on Saturdays or Sundays. Sessions are long and we must make some arrangement whereby Members can be home-and be home, one might say legitimately. In other words we must set proper times for adjournment. The people who can slip home on a Thursday or a Friday-and it is not my business when they go-should not constantly be at an advantage compared with those who have to travel over longer distances.
If the measure with respect to the proliferation of committees is passed, as I predict it will be, we shall have even more difficulty in the matter of attendance in the House. We shall have to be more mature in this country and realize it is not essential that every Member be in his seat every minute at every sitting. Of course, if this were the case in the British Parliament the chamber would be split wide open, because there is seating capacity there for only about half the elected Members. If there are a great many committees set up, then account must be taken of the circumstances.
The Prime Minister referred to horse and buggy procedures. I notice that an earlier leader of our party, Hon. John Bracken, as he now is, referred to something even more antiquated when we were discussing procedure in 1946. He said our Canadian practice was still in the ox-cart stage of half a century ago. So perhaps the horse and buggy stage represents an improvement.
I believe there are some more practical measures which could be taken in order to make full use of our time-measures more
1624	COMMONS
House of Commons Procedures practical than those which have been suggested. I think it is preposterous, the amount of time which is taken up by the voting procedures in the House of Commons. When one knows that at 9.45 on a certain night a vote is to be taken-and a Member may know this 10 days or even a month in advance-why should we go through the nonsensical procedure we follow at the present time? Mr. Speaker says: "Call in the Members" and the Members promptly go out and do not come back for half an hour. I wonder whether the statisticians have computed the number of hours spent in recent years while Members sat and waited to be counted. Simply being counted takes enough time, but waiting to be counted is an even less useful form of activity. I think we should look carefully and, I would say, hopefully, at the possible use of voting machines. Democracy is not thwarted nor diminished in those legislatures where they are used.
I think we should be able to find some means, in our collective wisdom, of providing against the so-called snap vote. I believe notice of such a vote, a matter of hours, should be given before it is taken. I believe -and I do not know how many of my colleagues would agree with me in this-that we should provide for those who vote neither for nor against a given measure. I have sat in this House occasionally and not voted. Once, I believe, a whole group did this. It is difficult to find that such a course is improper under our rules. It is probably more difficult still to justify abstention in these circumstances. But surely in a Parliament which has so many sides to it as this one-at least five- there must be occasions when an hon. Member would not think of endorsing a motion, yet would find the proposed amendment even more unpalatable. Should he not be able to indicate that he is present but that he does not approve of either of the suggested courses of action? Not everything is in black or white. Not everything is positive or negative.
It has been suggested there might be some danger attached to the use of machines. There is a story that in Finland a group of legislators, knowing that votes on three or four motions were coming up and wishing to vote against them all, broke a couple of matches and fixed the machine so that their negative votes would be registered, then went out of the chamber to drink beer. But surely our knowledge of electronics has advanced to a point where no real difficulty could arise. We need not be afraid of these devices, and I
[Mr. Macquarrie.l
DEBATES	May 25, 1965
think an innovation of this kind would increase our efficiency. Needless to say-and I am a traditionalist to the hilt-this would not affect our relationship with British procedures. Things are not done in this way in Westminster because, as I mentioned, there is not room enough in the chamber for all Members to take their seats and record their votes.
Looking through the record of earlier discussions on this subject I found a most excellent speech by a great Canadian leader, Mr. Brooke Claxton, delivered in 1943. He put forward some interesting suggestions, too. One was that by agreement during set debates such as the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne our speeches might be directed to one subject. We might have found it more helpful this session had we been able to do that, because we might at least have got our long delayed and much sought debate on external affairs. I commend these remarks of Mr. Claxton as being most fruitful. They were made in the course of a speech during the debate on the address, not during a discussion on rules or anything of that kind.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I note that the hon. Member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), I think it was-or perhaps it was a Member from the Government side of the House-mentioned the need for more research. This is becoming an important subject and a popular one. To realize its importance one has only to think of the size of bills which are presented to us. I believe there were 136 pages in the Canada Pension Plan bill. I studied all the Canada Pension Plans, and when I got to know them I discovered they had gone out the window and there was a new one being introduced. A tremendous amount of time has to go into the mere reading of bills. There is that dandy we are going to have on transportation. We have only to consider the Royal Commission reports, in their sheer bulk, to realize it is becoming extremely difficult for a Member, no matter how fast a reader he is, no matter how conscientious he is, no matter how much he burns the midnight oil for good and worthy purposes, to keep abreast of information and maintain effectiveness as a legislator and a representative of a constituency, without substantially increased research facilities. I welcome the developments that have taken place in the Library. We have a most excellent Library here and, in my opinion, a staff of great ability and extreme conscientiousness.
May 25, 1965	COMMONS
But we must have these services extended in scope and variety, and we must move closer,
I would say, in this instance to the American practice, where members are more adequately helped with research people under their direction in their own offices.
I would like to agree, too, with the hon. Member for Peace River on the question of a permanent Speaker; but I, like him, believe that the Speaker should be, first of all, one of us. I have never been enamoured of the suggestion of creating an artificial constituency for a Speaker, which is just one step removed from importing a Speaker to be our Chairman. I think he should be one of us, our elected peer to preside over our destinies and our deliberations with increased power certainly, and with that would come many improvements.
I am concerned about the very matters which the Prime Minister mentioned and which every Member has mentioned. We must improve our procedures; we must become more efficient; we must be able to arrive expeditiously at decisions. But as the Prime Minister mentioned and as others have pointed out, the right to be able to make a decision is not, in the final analysis, as important as the right of free discussion. If one infringes hurtfully upon the other, then it is surely the duty of anyone zealous of parliamentary	rights-and	parliamentary
rights is far more than a catchword; it is the essential, practical device of our democratic structure-to oppose it.
I will be very brief, Mr. Speaker, because I know my time has nearly gone, but in these measures I see three curtailments of the parliamentary rights of an Opposition. There is a restriction on the voting of supply. I may say that in this instance I like the amendment before us. This is an historic right, one especially cherished by the Opposition. There is also the oral question period, where the ministry is up for public and constant accountability to the representatives of the people. This is also a most valuable parliamentary device. One great scholar said that if he were asked to retain only one device to make a parliament free, he would keep the question period, where any Minister may be interrogated. I am concerned, however, with the suggestion that 30 minutes is sufficient. I think it is not. How many answers like the one given by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Beer) would you squeeze into a 30-minute period? When you do a little short division and consider five parties and five leaders,
DEBATES	1625
House of Commons Procedures five questions, five answers, you realize that you do not have much time left in 30 minutes.
There should always be the right of a Member to do what the hon. Member for Victoria did the other day, when he said, "Mr. Speaker,"-I paraphrase his remarks- "highways are as important to us as maple syrup was to other Members", who had wanted to raise that question. It is very important-it is essential, indeed-that representatives of all parts of the country be not denied, by the inexorable cutdown of the clock, the right to ask questions.
So I would suggest to the Government, Mr. Speaker-I see that the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith) is not here- that some consideration be given to finding an arrangement whereby we approach the shortening of the question period, because it has grown too long, but also to some device whereby greater protection is provided in this period. We must also have the right to vigorously oppose legislation for reasonable periods, because many times the interplay of public opinion has been directed upon legislation helpfully and usefully only because a decent interval has been allowed for public opinion to be enlightened and informed.
I would have thought-this, I think, is a very important matter-that in their suggestions for committees, and what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) called "ill-disguised closure", the Government would have moved in that direction with regard to Standing Order No. 33, which is the kind of closure that I saw from the gallery of the House of Commons applied day in and day out in 1956 under the brilliant efficiency of C. D. Howe. Why was not the suggestion made that the Standing Order that is to be adopted replace No. 33, instead of No. 6? If this goes through we will have one ill-conceived form of guillotine, and one standing stark naked, the one that was used in the pipe line debate. I should have thought the Government would have given a better impression of a real desire to improve procedures and retain the rights of parliament by having made that sort of application.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would say more except that my time has gone.

PRIVATE BILLS

speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, May 13, consideration of the motion of Mrs. Konantz for the second reading of Bill No. C-99, to incorporate Bank of Western Canada. [DOT] (5:00 p.m.)

maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are now taking up again, at this stage, the study of Bill No. C-99 entitled an Act to incorporate Bank of Western Canada.
I shall therefore take a few minutes to discuss this bill in order to make known to all members the position I intend to take with regard to our present banking system, as well as our economic system as constituted at present.
Mr. Speaker, there are now eight chartered banks recognized in Canada and since the beginning of this session, we have been submitted two pieces of legislation to incorporate two other chartered banks. One of them, Bill No. C-99, is now being considered.
During the last session we were also called upon to consider two private bills with a view to passing legislation similar to the one proposed under Bill No. C-99.
As a matter of fact, Bill No. S-6 which was put forward is pretty much identical to Bill No. C-99. I say pretty much identical, because I saw that a few changes had been made to Bill No. C-99, to incorporate Bank of Western Canada.
The bill now before us provides for a lesser number of directors or petitioners, if you wish, and the functions of each one have been changed to a large extent. Whereas Bill No. S-6 mentioned 54 executives, there are only 18 in this measure. Provisions have changed a little in this way; different people have disappeared and were replaced by new ones.
If you refer to the last page of Bill No. C-99, you will see that the authorized capital stock has been increased as compared to what was suggested in Bill No. S-6 discussed during the last session.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to explain my position in regard to Bill No. C-99. I wish to define it clearly and explain to the house that I am not against the chartered banks as such. Quite often it was said that the members of the Ralliement Creditiste were opposed to the chartered banks. That is not correct. Rather, we are opposed to the way they operate.
The effect of the charters which the banks hold at present, and which it is proposed to amend during this session, is that the chartered banks are granted rights and privileges which should devolve only upon the Bank of Canada, the bank of the Canadians, under the control of the Canadian government.
Mr. Speaker, it was stated that the new bank which it is intended to create could improve banking services in western Canada. But upon examining the figures which were quoted, we see that there are in Canada 5,500 branches of chartered banks, that is one branch for every 3,300 citizens.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the 5,500 chartered bank branches across the country are ready and able to provide the service which Canadians expect from chartered banks. Furthermore, I think they can increase the number of their branches in western, eastern or central Canada, if necessary.
Consequently, it surely cannot be argued that more branches will mean better service in Canada, because I think that the chartered banks we now have can offer the services required by Canadians.
I said earlier that I am not opposed to chartered banks as such, but rather to the fact that they are enjoying rights and privileges which should be the prerogatives of the bank of the Canadian people, that is the Bank of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I think that new credit has to be issued each year, because of the vast expansion of the country, in short, of Canadian business, trade and industry. Obviously, this means a greater need for credit each year. New credit is therefore needed, but under the existing Bank Act chartered banks -that is private companies-are given the privilege of creating this credit at will and for their own benefit. That is why I suggest that this privilege be only granted to the Bank of Canada, so that only the Bank of Canada, under an agreement with the Canadian government, may have the right and the privilege of issuing new credit according to the need of Canadian business, a need the federal government is in a position to make known to the Bank of Canada.
May 25, 1965
