Mr. Speaker, I do not object to the chartered banks playing the part of branches of the Bank of Canada in this issuing of new credit. But this should be done on behalf of the Bank of Canada, which would be responsible to the Canadian government. In this way, the Canadian government would control the issuing of all new credit, so as to ensure the good progress of the country's business, as it is indeed stated in the preamble of the Bank of Canada Act. At present, this control is granted only to the chartered banks, and that is why I suggest that we have now come to the point where we have a system that does not recognize the right for a human being to live a decent life in a country that can provide great wealth to all its citizens.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
A former premier of a Canadian province and former leader of the Conservative party -I refer to Mr. John Bracken-took part in one of the first federal-provincial conferences, in 1941, as premier of Manitoba. During that conference he stated that our financial system was designed in such a way that money was taken from the poor to be given to the rich.
Here is my interpretation of what that premier said.
Our economic system promotes debt-building in view of the fact that the government is financing public business by means of bonds and loans. It is not the poor that are buying government bonds, but the rich, those people who already have plenty to their names and who, in any case, carry but a small part of the national debt burden.
It is the richer class of people who own the debt incurred by the country through the chartered banks, and it is the poorer people who, in the form of very heavy taxes, must carry that national debt which is costing us this year over a billion dollars.
I think that the establishment of a new chartered bank, no matter which one it is, whether it is called Bank of Western Canada or anything else, would favour private interests and belong to a group of shareholders operating it for their own profit. I shall therefore stand against such a bill as long as there has not been a complete revision and consideration of the Bank Act.
That is why I propose, seconded by the hon. member for Beauce,
that Bill No. C-99 be not now read a second time but this day six months.
That proposal, Mr. Speaker, is in order to give the hon. members an opportunity to
make a detailed study of our banking and economic system in order to understand it clearly and in every respect.
When you talk to people you realize that very few are aware of that economic system. People suffer its consequences, but do not realize its implications.
If the bill were read a second time this day six months we would have the chance to clear up the matter of the Bank Act which must be renewed this year and to take a closer look at the banking system.
If you take a look at our government legislation today, you realize that everything is increasingly channelled toward that system of private enterprise which controls the economic blood of the nation. For instance, let us look at what happens when the farmers, at some point during their lives, must bring about certain developments in their organization. To have the right to improve their farms, to develop their herds, to purchase new machinery, to enlarge or improve their buildings, farmers nowadays have to ask permission from the banks. If they are not on good terms with their bank manager they might be turned down, thus having to apply to other loan sources and to delay or even give up their development plan.
On the other hand, we see young farmers who, to be able to continue their education, must also conform to the requirements of chartered banks. Over four or five years they have to repay close to $2,000 in interest to chartered banks to take advantage of the loans to students programs. But who will profit from it? Once again, those private interests: the chartered banks.
The same thing goes for Canadian fishermen. There is an act on fishing operations. Fishermen who want to improve their business, their boats, their fishing gear, their equipment are compelled once again to comply with the requirements of chartered banks and to give part of their income to private banks.
There is another rather recent measure, the Farm Machinery Syndicates Credit Act, under which a group of three, four farmers or more are allowed to buy quite expensive equipment. But, here again, to be in a position to take advantage of this legislation and to buy the necessary machinery to produce foodstuffs, farmers must pay a return to chartered banks.
I have only mentioned four examples of our laws channelling part of the income of our farmers, fishermen and young students toward chartered banks.

In my opinion, if we study our system thoroughly we will surely find a way to improve our situation so that farmers, fishermen, miners and all those who take an active part in the production, that is the producers of our country's wealth, become the owners of that wealth and profit by it, and not those who regulate and control the "sign" between production and consumption; something must be done to put this "sign" into the hands of every consumer, every Canadian, of all those who make up this country of ours, who built it.

(2)	During routine proceedings a Minister of the Crown may request that the question of allocation of time for consideration of any item of business or stage thereof be referred to the Business Committee for consideration and report, and upon such request being made such question shall stand referred to the committee.

(4)	If the Chairman of the Business Committee reports that the committee has unanimously recommended an allocation of time for the item of business or stage thereof, a Minister of the Crown may without notice propose a motion, to be decided without debate or amendment, for concurrence in the report, and, if agreed to, the motion shall have the same effect as if it were an order of the House.
(5)	If the Chairman of the Business Committee reports that the committee has been unable to reach a unanimous agreement or if the committee fails to report within the time specified by Section (3) of this Standing Order, a Minister of the Crown may give notice that at the next sitting of the House he will move that an order be made allocating the time for the item of business or stage thereof.
(6)	A motion of which a Minister has given notice under Section (5) of this Standing Order shall be made during routine proceedings. Unless the debate on the motion has been previously

concluded, Mr. Speaker shall at fifteen minutes before the expiry of the time provided for Government business in such sitting interrupt the proceedings and forthwith put every question necessary to dispose of the main motion. A motion requesting allocation of time, if agreed to, shall have the same effect as if it were an order of the House.-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to the record we are now on the so-called fourth day of this discussion about a Government- resolution to amend certain rules and procedures of this House; however, it should be pointed out that relatively few people have spoken. During my absence last week I had the opportunity of reading all the speeches made by hon. Members on this subject. I must say that I cannot agree with all that has been said.
A great deal of the four days has been spent on a philosophical dissertation in respect of parliament, at times touching upon the purposes of parliament. In this regard I believe that a great deal of the so-called public agitation which exists has been created by inspired movements on the part of the press and others in an attempt to persuade parliament to act as a board of directors.
It has been pointed out by some of the hon. Members who have spoken before me during this debate that parliament is a place for the exchange of ideas and a forum for the discussion of those ideas. It has also been pointed out that parliament is a forum for the examination of government action; for the discussion and examination of government expenditure, and last but not least, a forum for the granting of supply to Her Majesty. All too often the purposes of parliament are lost, and all too often some people adopt the belief that even though opposing ideas or views are expressed vigorously and tenaciously, no further expression or idea may be heard or considered.
There must be a full and thorough examination of all the business conducted by parliament. Parliament does not in itself exist to absolutely block or reject proposals. There have been incidents during the history of parliament, not only here but in Westminster which, had it not been for determined opposition to government proposals, would have ended with bad proposals in their original forms being inscribed in the statute books both here and in Great Britain. This same situation can be applied to the parliaments of any other democratic countries.
In this regard, Mr. Speaker, I put forward at the outset a caveat to the suggestion that everything must be cut and dried, and that
House of Commons Procedures discussion of ideas must be locked within the four corners of a limitation of time. This may be a somewhat strange simile, but it is apparent that discussion and consideration can be hammered into or fenced in within four corners of a timetable. I do not suggest that I am coining a new phrase when I say that in respect of the proposals now under discussion, and the proposals that will be discussed in the future regarding rules and procedures in this House, the Government is for some reason or other seeking to govern my ministerial railway timetable.
We have a proposal before us which deals primarily with a consideration of the estimates, and the allocation of time for debate to be affixed by a so-called Business Committee. We also have before us a proposal which deals with the powers of Mr. Speaker, and I should like to say more about that at a later time. The proposal in respect of the limit of time for debate on the estimates imposes a 36 day limit, and includes the consideration of the main estimates, supplementary estimates, interim supply and, for some unaccountable reason, it also includes the six supply motions, which have nothing to do with a detailed discussion or examination of the estimates.
The debate and consideration of the six supply motions, depending upon the generosity of the Opposition, could use up 12 days of the 36 days allowed for the consideration and debate of all the main estimates, supplementary estimates and interim supply.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
I am reminded of that time when some of the leaders of the Government were in Opposition; that is, after 1957. It was a strange and rare occasion when they did give up a supply motion. They insisted upon their rights. This was not begrudged in any way. Yet Parliament is now being put under the whip, if not cajoled, to reduce the number of days because there will be pressures from other quarters. Since when has an aura of sanctity descended upon hon. Members opposite? Have they suddenly become anointed that theirs should be that privilege? I would say not, Mr. Speaker. I would hope and trust that the Government would receive favourably the recommendation from Members on this side of the House that the 12 days allotted to supply motions be removed from the 36 days. I think we would see more nearly eye to eye if they did.
I also find that there is a trap in the 36 days, as was pointed out by the hon. Member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson), with regard
1636	COMMONS
House of Commons Procedures to supplementary estimates, and particularly final supplementary estimates. I would say to hon. Members on the treasury benches that, as previous administrations have, they can readily run into emergencies where the only way the emergency can be dealt with is by a supplementary estimate. For instance, there may be a crop disaster in Western Canada requiring that assistance be given to the farmers who are suffering from the ravages of the climate, or emergency action may have to be taken immediately in some other region. This is done through the medium of a supplementary estimate. But if the 36 days have expired or are about to expire consideration of the emergency action that must be taken is precluded or is engaged in only at the expense of consideration of other matters of Government business.
Therefore it is my view that the 36 day limitation on estimates is a boobytrap. Not only is it a limitation on the Opposition but it can impose a very serious limitation on the Government. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I would have thought that the proposal contained in the 18th report of the Committee on Procedure, which involved a flexible formula guaranteeing at least one day's discussion of the estimates of every department in formal sittings of the House, was far better. The present proposal is no guarantee that we will not have the same pell-mell, helter-skelter rush at the end of a session to drive through the estimates. It is very easy to take 20 days or 22 days on more noncontroversial departments. Government Members, by taking their regular time, not extraordinary time, can take up the fully allotted time, or even more, on these matters with the result that when the controversial items come up for discussion there is no time. This is why I say this proposal is an injustice to Parliament. It is an injustice not only to Members of the Opposition but to Government backbenchers.
As I said, the proposals for the amendment of the rules of this House in the last 50 years have been legion. In reading the speeches made so far I noted that the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) referred to the proposals of 1955. The recommendations made at that time were far reaching, but not too many of them were adopted. But every time there has been the adoption of a rule of limitation it has been for the benefit of the Cabinet, for the benefit of the executive.
It is within the memory of many Members of the House that not so long ago the debate

DEBATES	May 25, 1965
on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne was without limit. It was not so long ago that there was no limit on the length of speeches and, as has been pointed out, sessions in those days were not extraordinarily long. As a matter of fact, they were shorter than they are now. I would say that the fixing of a maximum time on speeches means that the maximum becomes the minimum. On many occasions we now have difficulty keeping within 40 minutes. I trust I will not transgress in that regard tonight. The institution of set piece debates such as those on the Speech from the Throne and the budget has been an intrusion into the right of discussion of private Members for the benefit of the Cabinet. We now have proposed a further intrusion into the right of discussion, a limitation of the debate on estimates. I wonder whether it will make Parliament more efficient.
We talk about getting things done more quickly. That depends upon whether the estimates will be sent to the committees early. There is nothing in the proposals to guarantee, and I mean guarantee, the setting up of the committees early in the session. The recommendation of the Committee on Procedure was that the Striking Committee should report by the 10th sitting day. As has been the case before, the present proposal calls for "with all convenient speed". Yet when the present administration was so anxious in 1964 to get on with the tremendous amount of business they took 8 to 10 weeks to name the committees. The initiative rests with the Government to name these committees. So what do we gain? There is nothing in the proposed changes which will speed up the naming of the committees.
The Committee on Procedure also recommended that the members of committees be named for the life of a parliament. There is nothing in that regard included in these proposals. If that were done we could really move forward and develop a corps of men who would be informed in their subject. We agree that the number of members on these committees shall be more limited. Yet we have to go through the business of renaming them every year, another step which permits of delay. The Government's proposal is entirely devoid of any assistance in this regard. Worst of all, you can name all the committees you want early in the session, but if you do not have the facilities for them to do their work, what are they going to do?-serve by standing idly by? That is precisely the situation today.

[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
True enough the proposal is for 22 committees. They will not get all the estimates immediately; but even now, with 10 departments available for reference to committees, I will wager that if those committees were named tomorrow no more than five or six could do their work. We have not got the clerical staff in the committees branch. We have not got the reporters. We have not got the translators. We have not got the committee rooms. Hon. Members will not sit on Monday mornings. Unless there is a complete revision or review by hon. Members as to what they are going to do with regard to attendance in committees, you will have difficulty in getting a quorum and getting effective work done.
It strikes me that this is, in some sense, trying to deal with the increasing toll of highway fatalities by merely making the speed laws somewhat tighter. It is not going to improve at all the driving habits of the users of the road. Until they do so and become more safety conscious we will continue to have a rising number of accidents and highway fatalities. The same principle applies. In addition, notwithstanding all the consideration of estimates before committees, there could still be, as I said, that pell-mell, helter-skelter dealing with estimates in the last few days and hours of a session. A government might call a department, have it on for a short day and then remove that department from consideration and bring in another one. The controversial matters will be left to the end.
It is true that estimates can be considered more effectively, I think, in a committee, provided the work is done properly. I do not believe a department has to go through an exhaustive committee examination every year. Perhaps once in three years would be sufficient, but let us see it. The Government complains about the lack of progress, but let us look at the number of committees that were not called in the last two years. The estimates committee, which in previous years had done excellent work on a number of departments to the gratification of officials and the government, was not called once by this administration. It is a disgrace. I say, therefore, that the Government proposal is no guarantee at all that the study of estimates will be any more effective. All it is is setting up a tight box, an infringement of the rights of Members of Parliament on both sides of the House for the benefit of Cabinet.

The hon. gentleman appreciates that my time is limited. If I could get the attention of the House for a few minutes more, I should like to discuss one other matter. I am going to deal with the abolition of appeals. It is true this provision is not included in the first part of the resolution, but so much reference has been made to it that perhaps the Chair will grant me this latitude. Personally, I am in favour of the abolition of appeals from the Speaker's rulings. I trust hon. Members will not feel that I am approaching this matter from a subjective point of view.
However, I do find it somewhat touching that the present administration should bring forward this proposal and that the Prime Minister, in his remarks, indicated that there was a growing trend to use this as a political or tactical tool. I am sure he knows whereof he speaks. If there ever was one flagrant example of it, I think hon. Members who were here on that occasion will remember it. It dealt with the question of whether or not there was an appeal from Mr. Speaker's decision under Standing Order 26 for the adjournment of the House. We saw the majority of the present Cabinet, and many of their followers as well as hon. Members in the third party, on a certain occasion solemnly vote in support of the proposition that such an appeal lay. It was an exercise, not in defence of jurisprudence or any logical argument, but merely a display of political muscle on a certain day early in 1963.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
But what made it such an apparent example of using the appeal as a political or partisan tool was that within a matter of a few months-I would say less than four months-when this administration had taken power they all solemnly stood up and voted that there was no such appeal.
Not only was that an exercise in hypocrisy, it was cynical.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME

It was contemptuous and it was contemptible. It was cynical in that it was repeated on a number of occasions. It was contemptuous of the Chair because it brought the Chair into a political wrangle, not only on that occasion but on subsequent occasions. Also I think it was contemptible in that it was an abuse of the rules and privileges of the House.
I have not said anything about this before, but I would say that if anybody displayed a

DEBATES	May 25. 1965
cynicism for the powers and rights of the Chair it was on that occasion. I would say that there should not be an appeal from Mr. Speaker's ruling. If Mr. Speaker misconducts himself-and such occasions are very rare in this House and elsewhere-a motion for censure can be introduced. The proposers of the motion, those feeling aggrieved, have an opportunity to put forward their points of view, and Mr. Speaker's decision may also be defended.
But as it stands at present, according to Standing Order 12, when Mr. Speaker makes a ruling on a point of procedure he exposes his flanks to an appeal that does not have to be justified; that whether it is frivolous or otherwise brings down no censure on those appealing; and all too often-I would say in nine cases out of ten-the appeal is misconstrued. It is no longer a question of procedure but goes to the substance, and therefore certain political positions and postures are taken.
Here I am not finding fault with any particular side of the House. Ridiculous postures have been adopted generally around the House, and I am speaking subjectively as the individual who at that time, Sir, was occupying the position you are now. This is the only reference I have made back to my tenure of the Speakership, and I must say I felt sore at heart there was so little regard paid to the position and dignity of the Chair. If anything has suborned the authority of the Chair it is indiscriminate use of the appeal, and it is for that reason I would say it should disappear.

True enough there is some danger, and I think hon. Members hold a bona fide belief that this might give too much power to the Speaker, and that by creation of precedents wrong practices might arise. If that were the case I would put forward for discussion an alternative based on the practice in the West German parliament where a small committee from all parties, composed of those who are versed in the rules, is a standing committee of the House on procedure.
May 25, 1965

If we had such a committee, and if a question were decided de novo, or if it were perhaps a rare occasion-and, Mr. Speaker, as you and I know there are many rare occasions for some rulings-if, say, a minimum number of Members, 10 or 15, were aggrieved, they could request that the matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Procedure which would examine it, and bring back a recommendation to the House that in future should such and such a point arise the matter would be decided thusly. This would be a safety valve against bad precedents on procedure. I put this forward as an alternative to see whether one can temper some difficulties of an absolute ban on appeals from Mr. Speaker's rulings.
For the third aspect of my discussion tonight I wish to deal shortly with the proposal for the establishment of a Business Committee. This is merely selective closure and is the result of trying to import into our Canadian practice a seldom used device of the British Parliament. I refer to the allocation of time order which is brought in under entirely different circumstances.
A Government House Leader who knows his business and is prepared to be tactful and be a proper Government House Leader can, with the other House Leaders, deal with about 90 per cent of the business of the House on a reasonable timetable. Mind you, there have to be some safety measures in that all discussions within the House Leaders' committee are privileged, off the record, confidential and that people must not, as was done on a regrettable number of occasions in the past, rim from such meetings to the press to disclose what may have transpired, or to leak what may have transpired at the meeting.
This method of selective closure is an attempt by the administration to choke off full discussion of controversial proposals in that a time limit will be set beforehand. Already a number of difficulties have been mentioned. No clarification has been given as to whether this will apply to a whole item of business or one stage thereof.
We have already made some progress in our procedure relating to the resolution preceding a money bill. Discussion on that stage is now limited to five hours. This is on a trial basis and we shall have to keep it in practice for a couple of years to see how it works. So far it seems to have worked reasonably well; but under the new suggested procedure a Minister of the Crown may stand up and ask that the whole of a bill, second reading, com-

There are many examples of unexpected amendments. The difference between the practice here and the practice in the British House is that, there, notice must be given of amendments and Mr. Speaker can disregard amendments as he sees fit. Certainly any House Leader who does not know what amendments are to be put forward will be chary of consenting to a time limit being placed on the discussion of any bill. And if there is failure to agree, one House Leader can impose his will. Then we get one day's discussion-a Wednesday, maybe, when the normal time for discussion is an hour and a half. Why, the Prime Minister rising in his place could utilize all the available time. Certainly the third, fourth and fifth parties would never get a chance on a short day.

How many people would constitute a party so that they might have the opportunity to go into a House Leaders' business management group or Business Committee? speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject of the rules and procedure of this House is of intense interest to quite a number of Members. It has always been of interest to me, because the rules and procedure deal with the fundamentals of the operation of this chamber. I have always considered that the rules, under the careful guidance of the Speaker, are very largely for the protection of individual Members of this House so they may have the opportunity to express their opinion without being dragooned into submission by the Government side.
Over the years a great deal of time has been spent on the question of rules and procedure. You have only to read Hansard of years ago to discover that the subject of parliament and how it should conduct its business has engaged the attention of the leading Members of the House of Commons from time to time. It is not anything new to have criticism of parliament. We were subjected in 1952 to a whole series of newspaper articles criticizing the parliament of that particular period, and I recall that when we had the Rules Committee of 1954 and 1955 we took into account some of that criticism. A lot of it was uninformed. There was similar criticism of parliament back in 1903, and I suppose no year has gone by when people have not criticized parliament. Very frequently it has been criticism by people outside parliament who do not understand the operation of this institution; and some of them, I fear, are not too keenly aware of the importance of parliament.
The regret I have at the present time is that over the last two or three years Members of the House have themselves indulged in what I consider to be rather careless criticism of this institution. They have encour-
May 25. 1965

House of Commons Procedures aged people outside the House to add their criticism of this place, and it has done some damage to parliament. I think this should be corrected and the basic factors underlying the purpose of parliament should be better understood by the people of this country. I feel there is a great misunderstanding of parliament, and consequently a great deal of serious and uninformed criticism.
Parliament is described as being inefficient, its rules and procedure obsolete, its organization of business antiquated: and "reform of Parliament" is today's catch phrase. People say that the sessions last too long, that Members talk too much, that speeches should be shorter, that time limits should be imposed before debates are commenced; and we are repeatedly told, "Streamline the procedure and get down to business". The weakness of this criticism is based on a misunderstanding of the function of parliament. It has been said many times, but it deserves repetition, that parliament is not an administrative body; it is a place for debate. We look to the cabinet and to the civil servants to carry out administration. Twenty departments have been set up for this purpose and thousands of civil servants are employed to carry on the day to day work.
Parliament's duty is to examine government policy, its taxation and spending programs, and its legislative programs. The government calculates the amount of money required for each fiscal year; it determines how that money may be raised by taxation, how it shall be spent, and presents to parliament its plans for so doing. The government draws up the bills amending the present statutes or introducing new measures; the Members of Parliament examine these various measures or proposals, criticize them, attempt to amend them or have them withdrawn, or to defeat them. The method is by debate; it is the only course open to us.
When a subject is highly controversial, the debate will be long and at times acrimonious. When a subject is non-controversial the debate will be short and without any fireworks. Some bills pass the House in a few minutes or a few hours; others take days or weeks. Some departmental estimates require just half a day; others may stretch out for from three to seven days. When the Government requested authority for the participation of Canadian forces in Cyprus a year ago, the House recognized the urgency and importance of the enterprise and settled the matter in a very short period. Members refrained from debate. But when a new

flag was proposed last year, rejecting the historic symbols of the two founding races, there was a prolonged debate which was brought to a conclusion by the imposition of closure. These two episodes indicate the contrast between controversial and noncontroversial issues. Controversy cannot be avoided in the House of Commons. Some people, including some Members of this House, said that the House of Commons should not be a political arena, but that the national interest should be paramount. That is unrealistic, because there are five political parties in Canada, not counting the Communist Party, each competing for favour, each with a program which its members consider to be appropriate in the national interest. Superimposed on the conflict of political parties there are marked regional differences which require and receive attention.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Members of Parliament may agree on some issues, but disagree on others, and parliament is the place for argument and the place where differences of opinion are aired and resolved. Parliament is the focus of public opinion, and government often has to modify or withdraw its proposals if the debate and controversy in the House of Commons discloses that the course of action should be changed. Those who talk glibly about reforming parliament sometimes overlook the purpose of the institution and seldom acquaint themselves with the facts. Those who say that parliament will accomplish more in a shorter period of time if all debates are limited in advance and if all speeches are shorter have not examined the history of Canadian parliaments.
If you, Sir, will look at the sessions from 1900 to 1927 you will find that in those days there were no time limits imposed on speeches. Members might speak for 10 minutes or for five hours, and some of them did so. The sessions on the average lasted for five months. The session of 1903 lasted for seven and a half months. That was a record not broken until 1961. In 1927 the rules were streamlined and speeches were limited to 40 minutes. That was intended to make a major change in the length of parliamentary sessions. If you will examine the period from 1928 to 1955 you will find that sessions lasted on the average five and a half months, in spite of that limitation on speeches in the House of Commons.
In 1955 the rules were again streamlined and certain major changes were made. Debate on the Speech from the Throne was
May 25, 1965

limited to 10 days, and later reduced to eight; the budget debate was reduced to eight days, and later to six; consideration of supply motions was restricted to 12 days in all, and speeches in Committee of the Whole House were cut to 30 minutes. Following those changes, the length of sessions from 1956 to 1963 averaged five and a half months, representing no change from the previous average from 1928 to 1955. A new record, replacing the 1903 session, was set during the session of 1960 to 1961 which lasted for eight and a half months.
If one ignores the sessions which sometimes start in the fall and run over into the next year, but examines rather the number of sitting days per calendar year, he will find that during the post-war period, that is from 1946 to 1963, the sessions of parliament have averaged six and a half months per year.
In 40 years the House has extended its working time by a month and a half. When our ancestors were here they were a hardier group and kept the House open for 31 hours each week. By the changes to the rules in 1955 we reduced the hours of sitting to 254 hours per week. I suggest that the proposal for reforming parliament, or streamlining its procedure-

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker.
I suggest that any proposal for reforming parliament or streamlining its procedure will fail if its objective is to shorten the sessions. The experience of 65 years, to which I have referred, indicates that Members will find some method by which they will be heard, irrespective of rules and regulations. My stand in respect of alterations to rules and procedures is in support of them, provided freedom of speech is maintained. The allocation of time by order of the House, and the imposition of closure, are means by which governments may have their way in imposing their wills, but the price paid is the restriction of freedom of speech.
It is not infrequent for a person inexperienced or ignorant of the subject under
House of Commons Procedures discussion to suggest that the debate be terminated, but it is even worse when a person who has already spoken during a debate suggests that everything has been said and that a conclusion should be reached. We have heard that suggestion frequently in this House. There may be Members who have a special interest in or specialized knowledge about a given topic who may want to be heard, but it is quite obvious that 264 Members cannot all speak about a subject, because very little could then be accomplished. Common sense prevails generally and the business of the House does get done; sometimes slowly, but sometimes quickly.
Each year parliament assembles and agrees on the Speech from the Throne, passes the Budget, grants supply to Her Majesty and enacts from 40 to 60 items of legislation; inquires into the administration of the departments, airs grievances, discusses private Members bills and motions, holds numerous committee meetings and generally considers in open debate with complete freedom of speech all the subjects that concern Canada.
There will continue to be pressure on Parliament to deal with the manifold subjects that confront it. The Government has grown in size and increased responsibilities have been assumed. A welfare state enlarges governmental problems, and to cope with all this parliament has to make adjustment from time to time. I suggest, Sir, that the frequent statements made to the effect that sessions are getting longer and that parliaments cannot get through their business do not stand up to an examination of the preceding 14 sessions.
I have before me a table in regard to 14 sessions up to and including 1963 which I should like to read. I will give the year, the number of sitting days and the number of bills passed. I intend to leave out appropriation bills which follow the passing of interim supply and estimates, which number on the average four or five per year. In dealing with the number of bills passed by the House of Commons during this 14 year period, I should like to read this tabulation, which sets forth an impressive record:

In those 14 sessions this House got through 654 bills, either amendments to existing statutes or new legislation. That averages 46 per session. So those people who say, first, that the sessions are getting longer and, second, that the government is not getting its business done have not in my opinion examined the record, because of those 654 bills who is prepared to say that some of those were unduly delayed or that the government was obstructed at the time the bills were going through? This may have been said when we were on the government side. It is being said when the Liberal Party is on the government side. But the facts bear out that this House passes an enormous number of bills each session and the facts indicate that the sessions are not getting longer. The session of 1903 was the longest in Canada's history until 1960-61, which was surpassed by the session of 1964-65; but I hope no one will ever take the session of 1964-65 again as an example of how to run a session of this Parliament.

I think that in non-election years parliament should have fixed periods of adjournment so that Members may know precisely when and for how long they will be in their constituencies. I think there is general agreement in the House with regard to that. I think that just as we have placed an over-all limitation on the Speech from the Throne, the budget debate and the supply motions, we should now set an over-all limitation on the estimates. Sometimes they have taken up to 60 days. My suggestion, which I made a year ago to the committee then sitting and have made since before the extension of the hours per sitting day was proposed, was that there should be 45 days for the main estimates, with an adjustment up or down on the basis of experience after we had tried it out.
I would be inclined to set 150 sitting days as the framework within which the business of parliament should be completed each year. Half of that time should be for government legislation, about one third for estimates and the remainder for the Speech from the

DEBATES	May 25, 1965
Throne, the budget debate and supply motions. I would hesitate to place any further restrictions on freedom of speech. Who is to judge whether a Member should be heard or should be prevented from speaking? If I want to discuss freight rates as they affect Western Canada, or the policy of Air Canada concerning its overhaul and maintenance base in Winnipeg, I must accord to others the right to speak about problems affecting their constituencies or their province. If a government insists on bringing forward some highly controversial proposal, it must permit full and free debate. Otherwise parliament is throttled or becomes just a rubber stamp.
No government in its senses would keep parliament in session for 11 months of the year as happened in 1964. If there is one thing more than another that Cabinet Ministers and Prime Ministers require, it is time to administer their departments and to develop policy with some leisure for thought. Without an interval of several weeks or months between sessions for planning and careful consideration, a government is likely to stumble rather badly.
I think that the proposed allocation of time in the suggestions put before us by the Government is a mistake. I am surprised that the Liberal Party, which gained some experience of closure in 1956, would be the party to attempt to introduce at this time another form of closure. Here again there has been some misunderstanding. Some accounts outside the House, and the odd statement within the House, seem to indicate that this is a normal practice in the British House of Commons and is worthy of adoption here. I realize that the proposal put before us is a modification of the British system. But when I heard about this matter a year ago when the Committee on Procedure and Organization was dealing with it I opposed the idea, and I very carefully studied the practice in the British House as disclosed in May's Parliamentary Practice, sixteenth edition. I read, I think, six of the debates in the British House on occasions in the last 15 years when they have imposed an allocation of time and I reached the conclusion that the British practice should not be introduced into this House at the present time, if ever. Mark you, we have closure on the statute books. It is applied in a different way in Great Britain. We have not given the same authority to the Speaker of our House that is enjoyed by the Speaker of the British House of Commons. With regard to allocation of time May says, as found on page 483:
May 25, 1965

An allocation of time order is not usually moved until after the second reading of a bill and often not until the rate of progress in committee has provided an argument for its necessity.
In other words, it is not determined in advance of the opening of a debate. As found on page 477, he has this to say, and I will not read it all:
-when, in order to secure the passage of specially important and very complex or very controversial legislation, the leaders of the House are confronted with the choice, unless special powers are taken, of cutting down their normal program to an undesirable extent, or of unreasonably prolonging the sittings of Parliament, or else of acknowledging the impotence of the majority of the House in the face of the resistance of the minority. In such circumstances resort is had sooner or later to the most drastic method of curtailing debate known to procedure, namely, the allocation of a specified number of days to the various stages of a bill-
Then he goes on to say:
This method is not provided for by the standing orders of the House but is applied, when the need arises, by special orders of the House known officially as "Allocation of Time" orders, and colloquially as "Guillotine" or "Closure by Compartment" orders. They may be regarded as the extreme limit to which procedure goes in affirming the rights of the majority at the expense of the minorities of the House.
Allocation of time was first introduced in 1887 and in the 76 years since that time the guillotine has been applied to 57 bills under successive Conservative, Liberal and Labour Governments. During the Labour Government of 1945-51, three bills were guillotined. From 1951 to 1962 under the Conservatives, debate on nine bills was thus curtailed. In 1948, for the first time, the guillotine was applied at the commencement of the committee stage. Normally it has not been used until after second reading, and after from two to five days have been spent on the bill in the committee stage. Then, on the plea of urgency and importance and obvious obstruction, the government has moved an allocation of time order. The order is debated for one full day, just the same as the proposal made here, and voted upon. If the government is sustained, the allocation of time is made.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
At that stage, a business committee is set up to apportion the limited time that has been allotted to the committee stage and subsequent stages. Now, what are the effects of these allocation of time orders? Sir Anthony Eden, when he was in opposition in 1948, when the House was dealing with an allocation of time order with regard to the Iron and Steel bill, referred to the experience of
House of Commons Procedures the House on the Transport bill and the Town and Country Planning bill in 1946-47, which were subjected to the guillotine in the committee and in subsequent stages. This is what he said in part on that occasion:
The Standing Committee on the Transport Bill had 31 sittings.. .At the end the position was that 37 out of 127 clauses and 7 out of 19 schedules had not been considered at all. On the report stage... the guillotine fell at clause 38 out of 127 clauses. The Government themselves introduced no fewer than 200 amendments in committee, of which 94 had not been reached when the guillotine fell.
Then he gives an example from the Town and Country Planning bill, and I quote:
On that there were 25 sittings in committee: 52 of the 108 clauses and 6 of the 9 schedules were not discussed-just about half of the Bill. The report stage ended when 14 of the 108 clauses had been discussed.
These two Bills were altered in another place by 230 and 336 amendments respectively.
We could, by this method, find extra work for the Senate to do, whose activities have been under scrutiny in this House during the last few days. Now, the experience of the United Kingdom is simply this, that allocation of time orders are infrequently used. In the period from 1900 to 1929, 32 bills were guillotined. From 1930 to 1962 only 17 were so treated. It is therefore a declining use in the British House of Commons.
Men of experience there deplore the use of allocation of time. In 1948, the late Herbert Morrison, who was House Leader of the Labour Party at that time, introduced an allocation of time order on the Iron and Steel bill. He was very apologetic about it and this is what he said as recorded in Hansard, page 1435:
I have said before that I do not like the guillotine procedure. It is a last resort, which is obviously necessary in this case. Nevertheless, I do not like it. I do not like moving it and I should not like to be a victim of it. I do not like the austere words of this motion, which sounds severe, when you come to read them in cold print. I shall not like the clang of the blade as it descends at 9.30 on certain nights. I should have preferred an agreed timetable such as was worked with some success...on the Government of India Bill-
Sir Anthony Eden, speaking in the same debate had this to say, and I quote:
How can the Minister tell us which parts of the Bill, when we come to the committee stage, will require more discussion than other parts? We may take a general view now on examining the Bill, but everyone who has served on a committee knows that the general view taken may be proved absolutely wrong when we get down to detailed discussion. All sorts of topics emerge that are not apparent when the Bill is first discussed.

House of Commons Procedures
Oliver Stanley, also a man of lengthy experience in the House of Commons, as reported at page 1534 of Hansard said:
Frankly, I intensely dislike the guillotine procedure in any circumstances... I learned that it was quite impossible for anyone, however well he knew the Bill, to lay down beforehand how the discussion upon that Bill in committee was likely to go and how long it would take or what time should be allocated to each part.
That, Sir, indicates some of the weaknesses of the allocation of time order imposed by governments who wish to exercise their will on the House of Commons. In a lecture given by L. S. Amery, another experienced House of Commons man, contained in a book published in 1932 entitled, "Parliament, A Survey," we find this:
The idea that a majority, just because it is a majority, is entitled to pass, without full discussion, what legislation it pleases, regardless of the extent of the changes involved or of the intensity of the opposition to them-the idea, in fact that majority edicts are the same things as laws-is wholly alien to the spirit of the constitution.
This, Sir, represents the experienced opinion from Westminster. This gives some indication why I have been opposed to allocation of time orders. I do not believe that freedom of speech should be so confined in this House. I am not of the opinion that necessity has shown that we require allocation of time orders. I do not like the Business Committee idea which apparently glosses over the imposition of an allocation of time order, but I do not want to deal in detail with that tonight because time is running out. We should be loath to indulge in a procedure which is recognized as a very severe form of closure which can effectively prevent debate. Once again I say this to Members of the House of Commons, over the last 14 years what items of legislation put forward by a Liberal or Conservative government have been unduly debated? Almost everything has been passed.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I think in the proposals before us we should attempt to narrow the differences by negotiation. We have had plenty of experience in the past in making arrangements by negotiation. A great deal of patience is required in this House on some occasions. 1 know as a result of the experience of being House Leader on the other side for three years that you have to be patient. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I consider that the citizens of Canada should be concerned not with the length of parliamentary sessions or the length or number of Members speeches, but rather with the function of parliament. I suggest, Sir, the average citizen of this country does not suffer at all when the House has lengthy sessions or when it sits throughout the night.
On the last day and night of the session which closed a month or so ago, some of us stayed here until three o'clock in the morning. Nineteen million Canadians were sound asleep in their beds and did not suffer one bit, but we were doing our duty here and
May 25. 1965

we sat those long hours, from eleven o'clock in the morning, through noon hour, through supper hour until three o'clock on Saturday morning, but no Canadian citizen suffered. In fact they may have benefited because we restrained the Government from certain actions it was attempting to carry out.
Citizens should be concerned with the policies of the Government, with the alertness and activity of the Opposition. For our system recognizes that to maintain freedom and our democratic way of life there must be an Opposition in parliament to restrain the government from arbitrary or autocratic action; to redress grievances; to check unnecessary expenditures; to disclose wrongdoing to public view and generally to express the varying points of view of freedom loving people.
For our system is founded on the freedom of the individual within the law. Members of Parliament are representatives of that freedom. Its maintenance is assured if it is the will of the people that freedom of speech be maintained. Restrictions rigidly imposed on that freedom in parliament would lead inevitably to dictatorship.

Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to contribute to this debate after the learned discussion which has preceded my intervention but I would like to say a word or two at this time. Following the very skilful speech of the hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and the speeches of other hon. Members perhaps I should not take part, but on the other hand I feel I would like to make a few general observations with respect to the nature of the resolution moved by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson).
The hon. Member for Edmonton West was very much concerned with the method under which committees are to be set up to study the estimates. He felt there was a danger in restriction of discussion on the floor of the chamber, but I was very much impressed when the Prime Minister pointed out that actually debating time will be longer in the House of Commons than hitherto. We will be sitting longer hours. We will be sitting through the dinner recess and at other times, and a longer period of time will be available to each Member of the House. I was impressed with the Prime Minister's argument and I feel that when committees are set up all the estimates will be given more attention than they have received in the past.
One cannot argue that no change is justified. It is commonly understood, from one
House of Commons Procedures end of the country to another, that our rules are antiquated and outdated. I felt a measure of personal satisfaction when the Prime Minister introduced this resolution to reform the rules of parliament in order to make them suited to conditions in 1965 because these rules, with few, small, rather insignificant changes, have existed ever since Confederation. The business that goes through parliament today is so tremendous, compared with that done in parliament in years long past, that surely it is high time the rules, after consideration in this chamber, be amended on the suggestion of the Prime Minister, who has assumed the responsibility.
I am wholeheartedly in support of what has been proposed. Changes may have to be made later on, and changes may be made before the resolution is passed in final form. I do not know that; but at any rate a great attempt is being made to create a lasting reform of the rules so that the business conducted in the House will be done in an efficient, modernized way, tailored to meet the problems that arise for parliament in the times in which we live.
I would not think of setting myself up as an expert comparable with others who have taken part in this debate. Accordingly my remarks are general in nature, but I feel I am speaking for my constituents when I say that long needed reform is at last being brought about by the leader of my party, and I am very happy to support this measure. I do not wish to be partisan and I will certainly try not to be but, as I said, I have a lot of personal satisfaction and some measure of pride in the fact that our leader took it upon himself to introduce this measure.
The opening words of the resolution are very meaningful:
That this House recognizes the need for improving its procedures to provide full opportunity for the critical examination of proposed legislation and to ensure the effective dispatch of public business.
I think most hon. Members are agreed that some reform is necessary. At present we have an antiquated approach to the dispatch of public business. Companies do not conduct their business as they did 25 years ago. They have changed with the times. Parliament must change with the times and I am impressed that we are trying to do the very thing which has been done in the United Kingdom, that Mother of Parliaments, which we all love and respect in our hearts.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
Something was said a few moments ago by the hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre
1648	COMMONS
House of Commons Procedures (Mr. Churchill) for whom we all have respect. He talked about freedom, and said it might be abridged. I would say that the true way to serve freedom is to make it effective, and the way to do that is to modernize the rules of this House and bring them up to date in accordance with the times in which we live.
Somewhere the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), I think it was, made a statement criticizing absenteeism in the House of Commons. I have not studied his exact remarks, though I should have done so before I referred to them, but I believe he said we were not attending the House of Commons as we should. It is my view that when the changes which are proposed in this resolution are brought into effect attendance in this House will be greatly increased. Prolonged debate, and too prolonged discussion of subjects which come before this House, cause absenteeism more than anything else does. Members of Parliament get tired of hearing the same arguments repeated over and over again by different speakers. I think these proposals will make debate more effective and result in more Members taking part for the benefit of our country than ever in the past, which is what all Members are striving for.
The Halifax Chronicle-Herald has an editorial on the speech made by the Leader of the Opposition. It strongly opposes the calling of the roll in the House of Commons every day as a means of dealing with absenteeism. The article says:
There always has been a prickly resistance among MPs to all suggestions that they follow the Senate's lead. Always, the roll-call idea has been dismissed without ceremony, and, we feel, justifiably. A full House every day would not merely fail to indicate that the nation's business was being conducted as best it might; it would be one proof, at least, that it was not being so conducted.
Finally, a roll call would be meaningless. After it was taken, MP's could desert the Commons in droves without doing damage to "good" attendance records.
I will merely say that I feel modernized rules would improve the attendance in the House of Commons. Modernized rules will make people respect parliament to a far greater degree than has been the case in the past few years. We must move with the times. We cannot afford the luxury of protracted debate. I think the suggestion that a Business Committee be set up is a good one. If the Business Committee cannot reach agreement unanimously, then a Minister will take the responsibility of moving in this House

DEBATES	May 25, 1965
that the debate be limited to a certain period. This is done all the time in the United Kingdom and I believe it should be done in this House.
In conclusion, in spite of all that has been said, there is not a single Member who does not want a reform of parliamentary rules and procedure. I am greatly indebted to what was said earlier in this debate by the hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre, whose study of the rules fills us all with admiration. I will say that. I feel he is giving us a lead.

speechtext:
I am glad to have this opportunity to take part in the present debate concerning proposals to reform and modernize our procedure. This is the first time I have had the honour and privilege of sitting in Parliament and I do not think either I or any other Member who sits in this House, especially on the back benches and especially if it is for the first time, will forget the marathon session of the twenty sixth Parliament, which set records we should not seek to match again.
The very even temper of this debate, the fine, balanced contributions from the spokesmen for the various parties in this chamber indicates that we have all reached a general understanding that reform of our rules is absolutely essential if we are to conduct our business not only efficiently but in a way which will permit us to serve the people we represent in an adequate manner. I was impressed by the contributions of the hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), the hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) and others who have spoken. It is clear there is a wide measure of agreement on what is to be done and I think the resolution now before us stands an excellent chance of being passed at an early date.
May 25, 1965	COMMONS
I had the privilege of serving on a municipal council. It was my introduction to public life and I learned the great value of the committees system and the work which committees could do. The reference of the work of the elected body to a committee at an early stage permits a much more careful and close examination of the business which has to be done. It does, or should, permit Members of the House to specialize in a few fields of interest and to follow in closer detail the work of one or two departments of government, and thus contribute to a better understanding of what is being done.
Not only must committees function effectively but there must be some discipline imposed on us as a legislative body in the conduct of our debates. I can remember that in the municipal council the great discipline which was frequently imposed was the discipline of the clock. As the hour of midnight was passed and the early hours of the morning began to go by it was frequently possible to get agreement as a result of the sheer physical pressure of exhaustion. I do not suggest this is a desirable way of getting agreement, but it did have the effect of permitting those members who wanted to say their piece to say it, while allowing council to reach decisions on the business before it.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
The elected body of this House numbers 265 Members. There is the double objective of providing the maximum scope for individual Members to have their say, while making sure that the debate does not exceed a reasonable length of time. We cannot have it both ways. It is not possible for every Member to speak on every subject and at the same time to keep debates within reasonable limits. It is apparent, I think, to many of us-it is apparent to me, in the short time I have been here-that a House cannot function without some measure of agreement upon the length of time of debates.
Closure is a clumsy and ineffective way of dealing with the problem, and after the unfortunate incidents of 1956 the government of the day, whatever its political complexion, showed an understandable lack of enthusiasm for employing the closure rule to terminate debate. I think it was clear on a number of occasions in the course of the second session of the twenty sixth Parliament that something akin to this kind of rule, or a reasonable substitute for it, as a procedure by which time could be allocated for each specific item had to be adopted, or else this

House of Commons Procedures Parliament would bring itself into contempt in the minds of a very large number of people in this country. In other words, Mr. Speaker, we have come through the process of going through the longest session on record, to some general measure of understanding of the minimum that has to be brought about by way of changes to our rules.
I suggest that the resolution before us is substantially the kind of thing which we all recognize must be. It is highly desirable that the spokesmen for the various parties in the Business Committee, to which reference is made in the resolution, be able to agree. There is no substitute possible for the voluntary agreement of spokesmen representing the different groups. As I say, Mr. Speaker, there is no substitute for this; but failing agreement there has to be some measure by which we can impose what is called in the British House the guillotine, however reluctantly we face this; however we know, all of us, in our hearts that it runs against the grain to cut off debate, to deny Members of this House the opportunity to speak when they feel compelled to speak for the people who sent them here.
Nevertheless the balance of interest has to be struck. We cannot have it both ways, as I said earlier. We cannot all speak on every issue. We must recognize that the business has to be conducted, and this is the most important priority. If after a reasonable length of time the procedure which is spelled out in the motion for voluntary agreement is not possible, the resolution proposes that an order for the allocation of time should ensue.
Parliament is a tremendous institution. There are those who would judge it superficially. There are those who would judge it by the attendance at certain times; by the amount which is contributed by way of debate, or not contributed; by external appearances-forgetting that behind all this is that measure of deep understanding of what is our primary purpose. Our primary purpose is to pass the items or reject the items which are presented by the executive branch to parliament. We must do this in an orderly way. If we fail to do this, then we bring discredit upon ourselves and upon this institution. The resolution in effect just proposes this, that parliament will agree to discipline itself. It can only agree to discipline itself if we all agree as individuals, as representatives of different groups, to a procedure by which the time allocated to debate is determined and that the vote shall then take place. It is
May 25. 1965

House of Commons Procedures a very simple concept and it is so fundamental.
It is strange indeed that I believe almost alone among the legislatures of the world the Canadian Parliament functioned as long as it did without something approaching this kind of rule or closure. Without applying either of these we did for a period of time manage to get through our business; but it was almost inevitable that without this kind of rule we would have what was produced in the second session of the twenty sixth Parliament; and a continuation of this kind of thing is not in our best interests.
There is one other small aspect of this matter on which I would like to comment, Mr. Speaker. That is the opportunities which emerge in different parts of the House to participate in public debate. With the multiparty system which is now being increasingly accepted in this House, the opportunities to participate in debate have been much greater, under the rules as they have existed up to this point, for representatives of some of the smaller groups; and the opportunities to participate by the backbenchers of the larger parties have been very few indeed. The mathematical distribution of time, in terms of the number of seats held in the House, or the proportion of votes taken at the last election, or any other reasonable criteria, is very much out of balance. It is very difficult indeed to be interested in the work of the House, to have prepared your material, to have speeches which you could have given and might have given were the circumstances otherwise, and yet to have no opportunity to participate.
The key to this is the reform of the rules. Without reform of the rules there is no equitable distribution of opportunities for Members. The key, further, is the effective
functioning of a committees system. Members of this House, through the committees device which is proposed in this resolution, and especially in resolution No. 15 which will be considered later, will be provided with an opportunity for participation in and review of estimates by the committees, will be a much fairer opportunity to indicate the talent which they have, the interest which they have and the energy which they can bring to bear in examining public affairs.
I believe it is now ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I rise on question of privilege? During the course of my remarks I was questioned by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) as to the first occasion on which there had been an appeal, under Standing Order 26, from Mr. Speaker's ruling. On that occasion the Minister suggested that the appeal had come from the official opposition. I would like to clearly point out that the appeal came from the hon. Member for Bumaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) and that he was ably abetted in that appeal by the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
